title: Follow Andrew around the Sea of Galilee

bethsaida.name: Bethsaida
bethsaida.text: John says Philip, like Andrew and Peter, was from the town of Bethsaida (John 1:44). The site is debated. Et-Tell, northeast of the lake, has long been the leading candidate, while el-Araj, closer to the shore, has recently gained support.

capernaum.name: Capernaum
capernaum.text: A fishing town on the north shore of the lake. Mark says Jesus went from the synagogue here to the home of Simon and Andrew (Mark 1:29). The ruins lie at Kfar Nahum in Israel.
capernaum.label: tl

tabgha.name: Tabgha
tabgha.text: Church tradition places the feeding of the five thousand here, on the northwest shore. Luke connects the feeding with the area of Bethsaida (Luke 9:10), and John places it on a hillside across the lake (John 6:1–3), so the exact site is uncertain.
tabgha.label: bl

bethany.name: Bethany beyond the Jordan
bethany.text: John the Baptist was baptizing at Bethany on the other side of the Jordan when Andrew first followed Jesus (John 1:28, 35–40). The location is uncertain. Tradition points to the Wadi al-Kharrar area near the river, east of Jericho.

jerusalem.name: Jerusalem
jerusalem.text: At the last Passover of Jesus's ministry, some Greeks came to Philip asking to see Jesus. Philip told Andrew, and the two went together to tell Jesus (John 12:20–22).

tiberias.name: Tiberias
tiberias.text: Modern city on the west shore of the Sea of Galilee, shown for orientation.

chapters.title: A fisherman from Bethsaida
chapters.html:
Andrew and his brother Simon Peter came from Bethsaida, a town near the north end of the Sea of Galilee. Like many families along the shore, they made their living by fishing on the lake.

Mark later places the brothers' home in nearby Capernaum. The ancient site of Bethsaida is debated, so its marker shows the leading candidate, not a certain location.
facts: Andrew is a Greek name, related to a Greek word for “man” or “manly.” Philip, also from Bethsaida, has a Greek name too.
The two main candidates for Bethsaida, et-Tell and el-Araj, are only a little over a mile (2 km) apart. El-Araj lies close to the modern shoreline.

chapters.title: We have found the Messiah
chapters.html:
Andrew was a disciple of John the Baptist. When John pointed to Jesus as the Lamb of God, Andrew and another disciple followed Jesus and spent the rest of the day with him.

The first thing Andrew did afterward was find his brother Simon, tell him the news and bring him to Jesus. Jesus gave Simon the new name Cephas, which means Peter.
facts: John says it was about four in the afternoon when the two disciples went to see where Jesus was staying (John 1:39).
The traditional baptism site lies about 1,250 feet (380 m) below sea level, in the Jordan Valley just north of the Dead Sea.

chapters.title: Fishers of people
chapters.html:
Walking beside the Sea of Galilee, Jesus saw Simon and Andrew casting a net into the lake. He called them to follow him and promised to make them fishers of people. At once they left their nets and went with him.

Jesus then taught in the synagogue at Capernaum and went straight to the home of Simon and Andrew, where he healed Simon's mother-in-law.
facts: Mark describes a casting net, a round net thrown from the shore or shallow water. Fishermen on the lake used such nets into modern times.
The remains of a fifth-century octagonal church at Capernaum stand over a house that early Christians honored as Peter's.

chapters.title: A boy with five loaves
chapters.html:
A large crowd followed Jesus to a hillside by the lake. When Jesus asked Philip where they could buy bread, Andrew pointed out a boy with a small lunch, while doubting it could help.

Jesus had the people sit down on the grass, gave thanks, and fed about five thousand men with that one lunch. The leftover pieces filled twelve baskets.
quote: Here is a boy with five small barley loaves and two small fish
facts: Only John mentions that the loaves were barley, the cheaper grain often eaten by poorer people.
The church at Tabgha preserves a fifth-century mosaic of a basket of loaves between two fish.

chapters.title: Bringing the Greeks to Jesus
chapters.html:
During the final Passover week in Jerusalem, some Greeks who had come to worship asked Philip to see Jesus. Philip went to Andrew, and together they told Jesus.

Andrew appears once more in the New Testament, in the list of apostles gathered in Jerusalem after the ascension (Acts 1:13). Later traditions about his travels and death are not found in Scripture.
facts: In each of John's three scenes with Andrew, he is bringing someone or something to Jesus: his brother, a boy's lunch, and a group of Greeks.
Jerusalem lies roughly 80 miles (130 km) south of the Sea of Galilee in a straight line.
